title: Field investigation associates norovirus GII outbreak at Chinese university with canteen dining - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The outbreak was reported from December 14 to 24, 2024, with the news article published on October 20, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred at a university in Jinhua, China, affecting students and staff with an overall attack rate of 0.48%.
analysis.event: A field investigation identified a norovirus GII.17 outbreak at a Chinese university, associated with dining at the canteen, and reported by the study authors in BMC Infectious Diseases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 215 cases were reported, with the first-floor canteen in Zone A having the highest attack rate (1.14%) and a relative risk of 2.71 compared to Zone C. Dining at Zone A canteen was the primary food-related risk factor with an odds ratio of 18.85. Poor hand hygiene was also associated with illness (odds ratio of 14.60).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation combined case descriptions, case–control, and retrospective cohort studies. However, it did not establish a complete transmission chain, and some positive samples could not be assigned a genotype. The study’s findings were based on the published abstract and are subject to further editing.

analysis.brief_en: A field investigation linked a norovirus GII.17 outbreak at a university in Jinhua, China, to dining at the canteen, with 215 cases reported from December 14 to 24, 2024. The attack rate was 0.48%, with the first-floor canteen in Zone A showing the highest rate at 1.14%. Laboratory testing identified norovirus GII in 16 of 66 samples, including six from canteen workers, two of whom were asymptomatic. The study found that dining at Zone A was the primary risk factor, with an odds ratio of 18.85, and that consuming more than three meals increased the relative risk. Poor hand hygiene was also associated with illness. While the investigation suggested foodborne transmission involving infected staff and subsequent person-to-person spread, it did not fully establish the transmission chain. The findings were reported in BMC Infectious Diseases and are subject to further editing. The study’s scope was limited to this university outbreak and available sequencing results, with proposed control measures including staff health monitoring, standardized work practices, and hand-hygiene promotion.

Norovirus, known as the 'winter vomiting bug', is highly contagious and spreads through close contact, contaminated surfaces, and food. The hospital established an incident management team to handle the outbreak. The evidence is partial, and the full original article body could not be extracted.
